REMARKS: On the above date and time, Airport Operations was notified by HPN ATC that an Embraer E175, Envoy Air Flight 3751 to ORD, had departed Runway 16 and reported a bird strike while in flight. Airport Operations Coordinator Jack Ciambra broadcast the alert notification, including all pertinent information, over Channel 1 of the Airport Operations radio. The ARFF team responded to the Runway 34 A-Pad and arrived at 0631L. Upon their arrival, HPN Tower provided Airport Operations with the aircraft's fuel status and number of souls on board, at which time Operations Supervisor Sean Kelly declared an Alert Level 1 over the 60 Control hailing channel. The aircraft landed without incident at 0647L, at which time Mr. Kelly cancelled the Alert Level 1 over 60 Control. The Pilot in Command (PIC) explained that while the aircraft was approximately 800 feet AGL, he observed several small birds strike the engine. Upon inspection it was determined that the strike did damage the fan blades of the number one engine and appeared to be an ingestion. Operations is awaiting an update from American Airlines on pending repair costs and aircraft time out of service. Operations coordinator Steven Serna conducted an inspection of Runway 16, which yielded negative findings. No injuries were reported. USDA Wildlife Biologist has been notified. There was no damage to the aircraft or operational impacts. The sample will be sent to the Smithsonian feather identification lab for a positive analysis. mor: ENY3751, E170, reported a bird strike on departure of RWY 16. The aircraft requested to continue until they check with their dispatch and then returned to KHPN as an emergency.  Runway inspection was completed after the initial departure and upon landing RWY 16. There was damage reported to Engine 1. REMARKS: N788CG was cleared to land on RWY 24 at ELM on a visual approach.  After touching down the tower had spotted a large bird on the runway around the 3,500 RWY 6 remaining point, abeam the compass rose.  The bird took off in an attempted escape, but was unsuccessful, the local controller observed a large burst of pink mist as the bird appeared to impact the starboard horizontal stabilizer of the aircraft.  The local controller reported the observed strike to the pilots.  The pilots did not hear or feel any impact.  The bird was observed in an injured flight state flying away at low altitude to the southeast towards RWY 5/23.  STY743, was also inbound on a visual approach to RWY 24 at the time and was sent around so a runway inspection could be conducted.  Airport operations conducted a runway FOD inspection and an off movement area search for the bird but were not able to locate it.  After returning to the hanger, the aircraft maintenance crew responsible for N788CG performed an inspection of the aircraft and reported no damage or impact stains.ASSUME 1 STRUCK This aircraft (N788CG) is not available for public tracking per request from the owner/operator.CORNING INC Unknown bird - large (Aves)

On May 18, 2026, I was serving as Captain on Flight 225 from JFK to TPA. During climb out from JFK, passing approximately 9,000–11,000 feet, the aircraft experienced a bird strike.  The bird impacted just below the Captain’s windshield, and debris from the strike traveled upward across the Captain’s window. Immediately following the strike, we requested a level-off and vectors from ATC to allow time to assess potential damage to the Captain’s windshield and evaluate for any other aircraft abnormalities.  Initial indications showed no visible structural damage and no abnormal aircraft indications. However, due to the System Operations Center operating out of the backup location in Woodbury, we initiated a SATCOM call to Maintenance Control (MCC) for further guidance. For approximately 10 minutes, we were unable to establish contact with either MCC or Dispatch. An ACARS message was sent requesting Dispatch to initiate contact with the aircraft via SATCOM.  We subsequently established communication with Dispatch via Microsoft Teams, and coordination with MCC was completed through that channel. Based on the absence of visible damage, normal aircraft system indications, and guidance from MCC, the decision was made to continue the flight to TPA.  As an added precaution, we elected to cruise at FL280 and 280 knots to reduce stress on the Captain’s windshield and allow for continued monitoring of aircraft performance.  The remainder of the flight was uneventful. The aircraft landed in TPA without further incident and was met by Tech Ops for inspection. Unknown bird (Aves)

REMARKS: American Airlines 1722, departing from KLGA RWY 31 to KCLT diverted to KJFK due to a report of a birdstrike and loss of the # 2 Engine. Subject aircraft landed at KJFK on RWY 31L and taxied under its own power to Terminal 8 Gate 4. Upon arrival, evidence of ingestion and damage was found on the #2 engine and inlet cowl as per AAL MX H.Abdelrahman. AAL FO S.L.McKnight advised that the birdstrike occurred on takeoff from KLGA RWY 31 at approx 400ft at 150-160kts. FO S.L.McKnight advised he observed approx 2 birds with CA R.Ioan. As a result, the aircraft will be out of service until further notice and passengers rebooked on another flight. The aircraft had approximately 17,300 pounds of fuel and 200 souls onboard. Aircraft diverted to KJFK due to loss of the #2 Engine and became Out of Service upon arrival. Passengers will be rebooked on another flight. There was no “loss” of the #2 engine…pilot pulled back the throttle to idle.  https://asn.flightsafety.org/wikibase/465881 https://www.nbcnewyork.com/queens/laguardia-american-airlines-bird-strike-jfk/6066775/ Smithsonian Wildlife/Species Identification: Canada goose (Branta canadensis) A321-231, Engine Manufacturer IAE Classification Standard Engine Model V2533-A5  At 08:30L one injured bird was observed in the RWY 4 safety area near the entrance of TWY G. 61SZ (Wildlife Supervisor) performed a hand-held euthanization. The carcass was disposed and identified as a Canada Goose.  AA operations and yes, the aircraft did make an overweight landing at JFK. MOR: THE PIC OF AAL1722 DECLARED AN EMERGENCY DUE TO A CONFIRMED BIRD STRIKE ON THE #2 ENGINE AND LOST POWER TO THE ENGINE WHILE CLIMBING OUT OF 020. PIC IMMEDIATELY REQUESTED TO DIVERT TO JFK AIRPORT. SOB: 200/FOB:17.3K. ASSUME 1 STRUCK. A320-232, Engine Manufacturer IAE Classification Standard Engine Model V2500SERIES  AIRCRAFT LANDED SAFELY AT JFK AIRPORT AT 0104Z. On the above date and time, Airport Operations was notified by HPN ATC of a Pilatus PC-12 who was reported to have a bird carcass hanging off the right landing gear. The initial report was from another aircraft on the ground at Westchester, who saw the bird hanging off the plane during touchdown. Airport Operations Supervisor performed a full length runway sweep of 34 with positive findings of a bird carcass at the runway intersection. After retrieval, the wildlife was identified as a Ring Billed Gull. Meanwhile Airport Operations Coordinator spoke with the Pilots of N438TW who reported that they hit the bird during their initial climb out from CYCL airport, which is in New Brunswick Canada. The wildlife was caught in the aircrafts right landing gear, and remained there for the duration of the flight. It wasn’t until touchdown at Westchester that the bird detached from the landing gear. Blood was later observed on the right landing gear door, strut, and on the underside of the right wing where the landing gear stores during flight. There were no known effects on flight, and USDA Wildlife Biologist has been notified. The wildlife remains have been bagged and are being stored in the wildlife freezer located in the ARFF garage. REMARKS: On the above date and time, Airport Operations was notified by Ramp Control of a bird strike on Envoy Flight 3499 from Chicago O’Hare International Airport (KORD). PAPD CASE 300249 PO 1063  Per Mary Hussey, GE Air Safety Investigator, the crew encountered birds upon takeoff and then 2 minutes later experienced noise, vibration, and low oil pressure warnings.  Within 5 minutes they shut down the #2 engine and then elected to dump fuel and return to JFK.  Blood was found on landing gear and fan abradable.  Two fan blades and fan abradable damage due to hard rub.  BSI found no damage with HPC.  Excessive debris with A-sump MCD (lab analysis confirmed Teflon/synthetic).  Engine removal declared and will be sent to MRO for repair.  CKK's spare engine will be installed on-wing (CVG OWS will perform engine change).

REMARKS: Alert 2 called for outbound Southwest Airlines flight 3711, pilot reported vibration in number 1 engine while retracting landing gear on take-off roll from Runway 4.  Pilots proceeded with a precautionary landing on Runway 4.  Aircraft returned to the gate under its own power and blocked in without further incident.  Upon inspection from Jett Pro maintenance representative Jesus Rodriguez, there appeared to be two bent fan blades in the number 1 engine.  No bird remains or snarge appeared to be present.  First officer N Michael stated, after retracting the landing gear on take-off roll he noticed elevated numbers on the vibration sensor for the number 1 engine.  He also stated he could hear an audible vibration noise until landing back at LaGuardia Airport on Runway 4.  Airport Duty Manager G. AAL958 told departure after about 10 minutes of troubleshooting, mayday mayday mayday and declared an emergency. AAL958 was vectored into Albany runway 01 and landed, taxied off the runway and waited on a taxiway for a period of time per their request. Eventually, AAL958 requested taxi to the terminal which they did on their own power. At the terminal, it was determined that there was no aircraft damage, but remains were found near the engine. AAL958 had 138 persons on board, and 3 hours of fuel.

REMARKS: While conducting a sweep of Runway 22R, Airport Duty manager R Dennis came across the carcass of a fully intact Rainbow Lorikeet by Taxiway K3. The Carcass was collected but no aircraft at this time has reported a strike or damage. night Google shows that Rainbow Lorikeets are only found in Australia.  Currently there are no direct flights from anywhere in Australia to JFK.  Qantas does have service into JFK (usually with a stop at LAX or DFW).  The only possible Qantas arrival came in at 16:58L on 22L (bird was discovered at 03:40AM the following day on 22R).  Other airlines (like Emirates) may have service from Australia to JFK but they would have to layover somewhere before arrival.  This bird is in decent shape which makes me believe that it wasn’t mangled/tangled in the landing gear of an aircraft. Runways 4L and 22 R were mostly used as departure runways leading up to the carcass being found.  The last arrival on those rwys were at 22:59L on 8/4. It is suspected that this is a domestic bird.

Smithsonian Wildlife/Species Identification: Osprey (Pandion haliaetus) Smithsonian Wildlife Identification Comments: Comparison of strike material with 20 publicly available vouchered specimens from Europe, Asia, and North America using COI barcoding gene demonstrates that the strike sample is consistent with the North American clade. REMARKS: On the date and time above, HPN ATCT notified Airport Operations that they received a PIREP about a bird on runway 16 just beyond the aiming point marking. Airport Operations Coordinator Michael Zaruma responded and performed a back sweep of 16 from taxiway Charlie. Coordinator Zaruma did not find a bird on the runway but witnessed and hazed two American Kestrels that were in the area. Approximately 30 minutes later ATC received another PIREP from an aircraft in queue on taxiway Lima. The pilot reported that they saw a bird in the grass that was struggling. Airport Operations Supervisor Adam Houghton responded to the safety area between Lima and runway 16, north of taxiway Charlie (Grid location D3). Mr. Houghton found a medium size bird in an agitated state with an apparent injury to its left wing (FIG A). The bird (believed to be an Osprey) was able to walk (FIG B) and was led away from the AOA and locked outside the perimeter fence (FIG C). No strike was reported by any pilot and no flight operations were affected during the time the bird was on the AOA. DAY. ASSUME 1 STRUCK. ONE PHOTO

While departing off of RWY 04L at 0535, JBU 1359 reported to ATC that they have encountered a bird strike and were returning to JFK for a precautionary landing. Upon inspection of the runway, the carcass of one Herring Gull was discovered near TWY K3 on the left side of centerline. Carcass was completely intact. JBU1359 returned, landing on RWY 04L at 0554 and proceeded to Terminal 5 Gate 25 under its own power. Met the A320 (N571JB) and spoke to pilot Gabe Mercado who stated seeing 4 or 5 birds near the approach end of RWY 04L. He says they felt the multiple bird strike on the takeoff roll and decided to return due to a vibration indication in the cockpit. JBU Mx Reylis and crew examined the aircraft and found damage to the #2 engine. Samples from inside the engine were sent to the Smithsonian for identification. ONE PHOTO Smithsonian Wildlife/Species Identification: White-headed gull complex (Larus spp) MOR: JBU1359 (A320)  DEPARTED 4L AND REPORTED BIRD STRIKE DURING TAKEOFF. THE AIRCRAFT RETURNED AS AN OVERWEIGHT LANDING AT 0951Z AND TAXIED TO THE RAMP WITHOUT FURTHER ISSUE. AFTER INSPECTION OF THE AIRCRAFT THE PILOT DISCOVERED 3 FAN BLADES DAMAGED ON THE #2 ENGINE.  Per JBU Safety team, No Airframe damage found.  The #2 engine required a borescope due to bird ingestion – no internal damage found. #2 engine had blade #22 damaged – this fan blade was replaced with a new one.  #2 engine had acoustic panel damage at the 9/10/11 o’clock positions – these panels were repaired.  #2 engine had attrition liner damage around the circumference of the fan case. All fan blades were removed and this damage was repaired.  #2 engine had a fan exit guide vane damaged at the 10 o’ clock position – the fan exit guide vane was replaced with a new one. The #2 engine was run at high power and no vibration or parameter issues were found.  The aircraft was out of service for 36 hours due to this event. MOR: JBU1359, A320 DEPARTURE OFF JFK TO MKJP, REPORTED A BIRD STRIKE AND DECLARED AN EMERGENCY DUE TO AN OVERWEIGHT LANDING.  27,400# FUEL 166 SOB. LANDED WITHOUT INCIDENT AT 0951Z.

1018L: Federal Aviation Administration Air Traffic Control Tower reported a bird strike for an inbound aircraft arriving runway 22 that resulted in a go-around to Port Authority Operations. 1025L KLGA 61 (TP) responded and conducted a special runway inspection of runway 22 full length where no remains were found. 1050L KLGA 61 (TP) responded to gate 43 for the strike on an EMBRAER S A ERJ 170-200 LR, Republic Airlines inbound flight 4535, from KOKC to KLGA. Republic Airlines aircraft maintenance, Armando Camacho Tzompantzi, confirmed three points of damage as of now to the aircraft and there was two strike points located. The first strike point was located on the number one engine inboard cowling resulting in a dent and crack that measured approximately 7 inches long and 1 – 2 inches wide. The second-strike point was located on the captain’s side main landing gear resulting in the main gear retractable door being bent and the landing gear forward rod being sheared off at the top half and bent. Republic maintenance will follow up with PA Operations if further damage is found and update PA Ops with the repair work on the aircraft. In the meantime, the aircraft is AOG and has been relocated to spot R2 until repairs can be made. Middle gear door and rod needed replacement as well. Inlet replacement cost = $724,950.00  Door Rod cost = $385 Middle door cost = $3278.48  TOTAL COST = $728,613.87 and time OOS was 110 hours for labor. I was operating CE-525B N225TJ as a single pilot-in-command on a part 91 IFR flight from KRFD to KHTO that struck two deer during landing at KHTO. The flight departed ahead of the scheduled time at 2048Z with a planned time enroute of 2:14 at FL390. The flight proceeded normally. At 7nm from KHTO, The flight was cleared for a visual approach to runway 10. The weather conditions during the approach were night VMC with calm winds. I touched down at approximately 1000-1200 feet from the threshold of the approach end of runway 10, selected ground flaps and began applying brakes. Slowing through approximately 60-70 (somewhere between taxiway H and runway 16/34) two deer appeared on the runway on either side of the centerline moving from north to south. I instinctively released the brakes, maintained runway centerline and when I was past the deer (I did not hear or feel any significant impact) resumed maximum braking. We cleared the runway on taxiway E, continued to the ramp and alerted an aircraft that was waiting to depart that there are deer on the runway and that we may have hit one. During the taxi in, I completed the after landing checklist (partially retracting the flaps and later returning them to the ground position). A visual inspection of the aircraft revealed impact damage to the right wing leading edge, evidence of an impact on the left leading edge (didn’t appear damaged) and both flaps suffered impact damage. FBO personnel cleared the runway of both deer carcasses and any looked for FOD. The airfield resumed normal operations after it was cleared. Performance Flight Group. EIGHT PHOTOS. EOF OTHER REPORTED AS The aircraft cleared the runway and shut down on the ramp.
COMMENTS: EOF OTHER REPORTED AS The aircraft cleared the runway and shut down on the ramp.

DAMAGING STRIKE REPORT / POST STRIKE INVESTIGATION:  A Wildlife Officer reported to the AAL maintenance hangar after being notified of an aircraft taken out of service due to a bird strike.  The call was received more than two hours after the aircraft had landed.  According to the AAL maintenance Lead, the bird strike was noticed by the outbound flight crew during the pre-flight inspection walk-around.  A very large smudge of blood was noticed on the cowling of the #2 engine.  The aircraft was immediately taken out of service for further inspection.  At first it looked like there was no damage to the fan blades or the engines.  However, when they opened up the engine, they were able to find 6 Outlet Guide Vanes damaged and 1 side panel damaged.  Aircraft was out for 24 hours before it returned to the flight line.  It is unknown where the strike occurred, since the arrival crew never indicated a bird strike in the cockpit log or mentioned it to maintenance personnel.  The lack of bird remains reported or found on the arrival runway, points to the STRIKE TAKING PLACE OFF AIRPORT PROPERTY.  DNA samples were taken to be sent off for positive ID and possibly pinpoint where the strike might have taken place.  LD. ASSUME 1 STRUCK.  FOUND KMIA. Smithsonian Wildlife/Species Identification: Double-crested cormorant (Phalacrocorax auritus) EOF OTHER REPORTED AS TAKEN OUT OF SERVICE FOR REPAIRS

No effect to aircrafts directional control, however aircraft was delayed for 1 hour for the replacement of the captains side windshield wiper that was damaged from the strike. Aircraft received new departure flight 5684 and a different aircraft was used. On 4/12/21, Wilson Piedra/RPA provided the following update on strike:  MX found the left hand windshield wiper cracked. Windshield wiper was removed and replaced. Approximate cost for the part is $2,121. There were a total of (2) mechanics working from 1447L to 1627L for a total of 1 hour and 40 minutes. Delayed for 1 hour for the replacement of the captains side windshield wiper that was damaged from the strike.
